prompt: Which two browsers draw pages with the same engine?
hint: Three engines draw almost every page.

choices.text: Chrome and Firefox
choices.why: Both are free and cross-platform, and Firefox draws with Gecko, Chrome with Blink.

choices.text: Chrome and Edge
choices.why: Right: both are Blink, which is why one stands in for the other at low depth.

choices.text: Firefox and Safari
choices.why: Gecko and WebKit: two different engines.

choices.text: Edge and Safari
choices.why: Blink and WebKit, apart from Edge on an iPhone.

prompt: Which engine has drawn Chrome on an iPhone for most of its history?
hint: Apple set the rule.

choices.text: Blink, as on every other platform Chrome runs on
choices.why: The name is the same; on an iPhone the engine was not.

choices.text: Gecko, borrowed from Firefox
choices.why: Gecko is Firefox's engine, and Firefox on an iPhone did not use it either.

choices.text: WebKit, Safari's engine
choices.why: Right: so Chrome on an iPhone sits closer to Safari than to Chrome on Android.

choices.text: A mobile engine Google wrote for small screens
choices.why: There is no such engine; the size is handled by layout, not by a separate engine.

prompt: R8 says 360 pixels. A phone's screen has 1080 physical pixels across. What width does a tester set in responsive mode?
hint: The unit a page is laid out in.

choices.text: 1080, the dots the phone really has
choices.why: Those are device pixels; the page is laid out in CSS pixels, three dots each here.

choices.text: 360, in CSS pixels
choices.why: Right: R8's width is the layout width, and that phone lays pages out at 360.

choices.text: 540, halfway, to cover both phones
choices.why: Neither phone lays a page out at 540; it is a width nobody has.

choices.text: 120, the 1080 split by the three dots per pixel twice
choices.why: Dividing once gives 360; dividing again has no meaning.

prompt: Fourteen cells, two weeks, and a morning per full pass. What is the matrix for, if not a list of work?
hint: What does a cell left out become?

choices.text: It makes every cell not run a decision with a reason
choices.why: Right: the choice becomes visible, instead of a browser nobody thought of.

choices.text: It is for the automation team, who run all fourteen cells overnight
choices.why: Automation is another course, and the choice still has to be made here.

choices.text: It records versions, since "current" moves every four weeks
choices.why: Versions are one more axis of the matrix, not its purpose.

choices.text: It is filled in by the client to say which browsers they want
choices.why: The audience and the risks choose the cells; the client reviews the result.

prompt: Match each dimension to what it changes.
hint: One right-hand side belongs to no dimension.

pairs.right: The engine that draws the page
The fallback fonts, and which browsers exist
The input and the size in the hand
The width the page is laid out at

prompt: Which two inputs choose the cells and their depth?
hint: One is about people, one about the product.

choices.text: The devices the tester owns and the time each one takes
choices.why: That tests the tester's habits, which the section names as the first poor choice.

choices.text: The newest version of each browser and its global share
choices.why: Global share is somebody else's audience; the theatre has its own.

choices.text: Who uses the product, and where it is likely to break
choices.why: Right: the audience says which cells matter, the risk how deep to go.

choices.text: The developer's browser and the client's browser
choices.why: Two people's browsers say little about seven in ten visits from phones.

prompt: Firefox brings 3% of the theatre's visits. Which reason does the lesson give for still testing it?
hint: Think about engines.

choices.text: It is the browser Ana uses every day
choices.why: Her habits are what the choice is meant to correct for.

choices.text: Any share above one in a hundred has to be tested in full
choices.why: There is no such cut-off, and Firefox gets a short pass, not a full one.

choices.text: It is the only Gecko cell, and every engine gets one
choices.why: Right: differences live between engines, whatever the share.

choices.text: It releases more often than the other three
choices.why: Chrome, Edge and Firefox all ship every four weeks or so.

prompt: The old site's statistics show almost no visits from Safari on Macs. What should Ana do with that number first?
hint: Who stops visiting a site that is broken for them?

choices.text: Drop the cell, since the audience has spoken
choices.why: The audience may have left because the old site failed there.

choices.text: Ask whether the old site worked there before reading it as a reason
choices.why: Right: the data describes who the old site worked for.

choices.text: Test it last, after every other cell has passed
choices.why: Order by risk is right, and it still skips the question the number raises.

choices.text: Replace it with Chrome on a Mac, which has more visits
choices.why: Chrome on a Mac is Blink, and the WebKit desktop cell would be lost.

prompt: What about boxoffice makes a modest matrix defensible?
hint: What does the page send to the browser?

choices.text: It sells tickets for only three shows
choices.why: Three shows or three hundred, the same page meets the same engines.

choices.text: It runs on 127.0.0.1, on the tester's own laptop
choices.why: That is the lab; the customers' browsers are the ones the matrix is about.

choices.text: Plain HTML, a short style block, and no script at all
choices.why: Right: two of the three sources of difference are small and the third is absent.

choices.text: It is a first release, so nothing in it can regress
choices.why: A first release has everything to test, not less.

prompt: However small its share, every ___ gets at least one cell.
hint: Blink, Gecko and WebKit are three of them.

prompt: Put the steps for checking R8 in Chrome in order.
hint: The width comes before the looking.
trap: Measuring before setting the width measures the desktop window.

prompt: What makes the home page wider than a phone?
hint: curl and grep found one rule.

choices.text: The page has no viewport line, so phones lay it out at desktop width
choices.why: It has the line; the second capture shows it.

choices.text: The table of shows is fixed at 760 pixels
choices.why: Right: table.shows{width:760px}, whatever the window.

choices.text: The page's margin of 16 pixels on each side
choices.why: The margin adds 16 to the width; the 760 is what does not fit.

choices.text: The dates are too long to wrap
choices.why: The dates fit inside the window; three whole columns do not.

prompt: From which window width does the home page stop scrolling sideways in Chromium?
hint: The page is 776 wide; lesson 4's boundary thinking applies.

choices.text: From 768, a common width for a tablet held upright
choices.why: At 768 the page still measured 776, eight pixels too wide.

choices.text: From 761, one more than the table's 760
choices.why: That forgets the 16 pixels of margin on the left.

choices.text: From 776
choices.why: Right: 775 still scrolls, 776 fits.

choices.text: From 361: only R8's width of 360 is affected
choices.why: Every width below 776 scrolls; 360 is deep inside the failing side.

prompt: The outbox scrolls sideways at 360 once it holds an e-mail. Why is that not a defect against R8?
hint: Whose page is it?

choices.text: R8 covers the home page and nothing else
choices.why: R8 says every page.

choices.text: It only overflows by 63 pixels, which is too little to matter
choices.why: A small overflow on a theatre page would still be a defect; size is not the reason.

choices.text: It is the test build's page, not one of the theatre's
choices.why: Right: the requirements are about the theatre's system, so it is a note.

choices.text: Long links are expected to scroll on any phone
choices.why: Expected by whom? The reason is whose page it is.

prompt: What does Ana write down while the defect is in front of her? Choose every one the lesson lists.
hint: Lesson 15 turns it into a report.

choices.text: The requirement, R8
choices.why: The report cites what the product departs from.

choices.text: The browser and its version
choices.why: Another version may behave differently.

choices.text: The width and the measured page width
choices.why: 360 and 776, numbers somebody else can check.

choices.text: A corrected stylesheet for Rui
choices.why: The fix is Rui's; the report describes the problem.

choices.text: The rule table.shows{width:760px}
choices.why: It shows where the width comes from.

choices.text: The number of seats left for each show
choices.why: Seats have nothing to do with the layout.

prompt: Which of these does responsive mode leave unchanged?
hint: Chrome set to look like an iPhone.

choices.text: The width the page is laid out at
choices.why: That is the first thing it changes.

choices.text: The engine that draws the page
choices.why: Right: it is still Blink, which is why Safari needs its own cell.

choices.text: The name the browser gives itself to the site
choices.why: It changes that too, to the device's browser name.

choices.text: Whether touch input is used
choices.why: It imitates touch as well.

prompt: Ana's phone is on the same Wi-Fi as her laptop and still cannot open boxoffice. Why?
hint: Read the address it listens on.

choices.text: Home Wi-Fi blocks port 8000
choices.why: Nothing about the port is the problem; the address is.

choices.text: It listens on 127.0.0.1, which means this machine
choices.why: Right: only programs on the laptop can reach it, an emulator included.

choices.text: Phones refuse pages served over http
choices.why: Phones open http pages; they warn about them.

choices.text: boxoffice detects phones and refuses them
choices.why: boxoffice never looks at the device at all.

prompt: Match each need to the tool the lesson gives for it.
hint: One tool needs a Mac.

pairs.left: Safari on an iPhone, with no iPhone on the team
Real Chrome for Android on the laptop
Every page at 360 on every new build
iOS Safari's engine on a Mac

prompt: A device cloud's tunnel would let its iPhone reach boxoffice on Ana's laptop. What makes opening one a decision rather than a setting?
hint: A path, and what is at the end of it.

choices.text: Tunnels slow pages so much that layout tests stop being valid
choices.why: Speed changes a little; the layout the phone draws does not.

choices.text: Tunnels only carry https, and boxoffice speaks http
choices.why: The section names no such limit; the concern is who gets in.

choices.text: The cloud has to be paid for each time a tunnel opens
choices.why: Prices are the service's business, and not the risk the section names.

choices.text: It gives an outside machine a path inside, to whatever data is there
choices.why: Right: test data only, and somebody allowed to say yes.

prompt: A colleague's report says "tested on mobile: passes". What would make that claim checkable?
hint: The last line of the lesson.

choices.text: A screenshot from any phone
choices.why: One picture with no device, engine or method named says little more.

choices.text: Adding "and on tablet" to cover the larger screens
choices.why: Another unnamed cell makes two unchecked claims.

choices.text: Which phone, which browser and engine, and how it was reached
choices.why: Right: a cell of the matrix and a method, which somebody else can repeat.

choices.text: A second tester saying the same thing
choices.why: Two people repeating the claim still do not say where it was checked.

prompt: Chrome on an Android phone has passed. Which cell next adds a new engine and the most customers?
hint: Use the audience table and the engines.

choices.text: Edge on an Android phone
choices.why: Blink again: little new to learn.

choices.text: Chrome on Windows, 13% of visits
choices.why: More customers than most, and still the same engine.

choices.text: Safari on an iPhone, 24% of visits
choices.why: Right: WebKit, and a quarter of the audience.

choices.text: Firefox on Windows, 3% of visits
choices.why: A new engine, Gecko, and the smallest share of the three.

prompt: Drawing a page in a desktop browser at a phone's width is what the browser's ___ mode does.
hint: Chrome hides it behind Ctrl+Shift+M.
